title: ENERGY-COMPUTE-MORPHOLOGY CO-OPTIMIZATION IN INTELLIGENT ROBOTIC MATTER AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名:智能機器人物質的能源—運算—變形協同極限 25/90 ENERGY-COMPUTE-MORPHOLOGY CO-OPTIMIZATION IN INTELLIGENT ROBOTIC MATTER AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition in the STARLI YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy (Research Institute XXXVI, Flagship 25 of 90). It asks whether an identified, modular robotic vehicle-body research section can jointly allocate electrical energy, real-time computation and physically verified morphology transitions without hiding external support or crossing a structural safety limit. The three-way research coupling is Energy Budgets x Computing Resources x Morphing Efficiency. All proposed evidence is restricted to unoccupied bench coupons, a prospective 24-module panel, calibrated electrical and mechanical references, and bounded hardware-in-the-loop tests. No completed full vehicle, passenger safety result or road certification is asserted. The falsifiable candidate is that, under matched material, complete rail energy, compute cycles, sensing, communication, time and human-operation budgets, a frozen co-optimization policy can improve the number of independently verified graceful-degradation modes without worsening a preregistered peak-temperature bound. Its strongest comparators are competently tuned centralized planning, energy-aware but mechanics-unaware scheduling and passive safe-hold modules. Blinded challenges include unnoticed facility power, processor deadline overload, buried connector hotspots, battery aging, stale measurement timestamps, dry-friction joints, infeasible load paths and unsafe intermediate shapes. The original seed's Miner fatigue model D_f = sum(n_i/N_i) is retained as one conditional life-cycle proxy, not mislabeled as an energy-optimization law. Thirty mathematically distinct research plates develop terminal energy integration, power continuity, Joule loss, battery state, converter efficiency, thermal transients, CPU switching energy, real-time schedulability and response time, stale-information age, queue backlogs, communication work, robot dynamics, actuation work, frictional hysteresis, kinematic singularity, elastic buckling, fatigue, feasible Pareto fronts, KKT-style constrained objectives, hard safe sets, barrier conditions, tail risk, correlated uncertainty, chance constraints, complete-denominator yield, stopping latency and conjunctive physical requalification. Each plate identifies units, assumptions and its own concrete blind falsification. Eighty-two chapters comprise 410 separately paginated investigations into electrical rails, scheduling, structural transitions, three-way constrained optimization, adversarial causal comparisons and cross-generation scientific transfer. Two hundred Research Gates present distinct physical questions, tailored fault interventions, causal rivals and noncompensatory stop rules; all failed, refused and unfinished missions remain in the evidence denominator. Thirty-three distinguishable Phoenix Answer Embryos propose future instruments, test fixtures and evidence packages with explicit ways to falsify or retire them. The book reports research designs and questions rather than experimental achievements. The scope is prospective, scaled and non-occupancy. Missing load custody, unmetered energy, stale authority, missed deadlines, undercovered uncertainty or unsuccessful physical stopping forbids release regardless of efficiency gains. Methodological DOI context includes Robo-Matter (10.1038/s41467-024-53123-6), flying-swarm shape assembly (10.1038/s44172-026-00715-3), real-time scheduling (10.1145/321738.321743), battery SOC estimation (10.1038/s44359-026-00145-6), modular reconfiguration (10.1007/s10846-024-02067-6) and dynamic topology consensus (10.1109/TAC.2005.846556), alongside author-supplied Flagship 13 research ancestry (10.5281/zenodo.23318840 and 10.5281/zenodo.23318839; metadata not independently confirmed here). External studies concern relevant components or theory, not validation of this complete F25 architecture. title: AI-Driven Generative Content & Predictive Analytics in Hybrid Academic Libraries: A Zero-Trust, Anti-Deviance Architecture
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract Academic libraries are undergoing a profound paradigm shift, evolving from passive hybrid repositories into autonomous, AI-augmented knowledge ecosystems. While traditional hybrid frameworks address basic print-digital coexistence, they suffer from critical vulnerabilities: high-demand resource friction, physical material mutilation, licensing piracy, unauthorized access, and algorithmic bias in digital discovery. This paper introduces a novel operational paradigm—the Zero-Trust Anti-Deviance Architecture (ZT-ADA)—that integrates Generative AI, Predictive Anomaly Detection, and Dynamic Resource Orchestration (DRO). Under ZT-ADA, predictive models anticipate resource surges during peak evaluation cycles, pre-allocating dynamic multi-user digital access and personalized generative summaries to mitigate physical collection stress. Simultaneously, a zero-trust cyber-physical verification matrix continuously evaluates access telemetry to detect physical deviance (mutilation, concealment, retention abuse) and digital breach threats in real time. We present mathematical formulations, operational workflows, risk matrices, and empirical evaluation metrics to establish a resilient, ethical, and scalable blueprint for 21st-century academic libraries.

title: Cyclical Force Generation for Triboelectric Nanogenerators: A Review of Mechatronic Approaches, Challenges and Future Perspectives
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) convert low-frequency and irregular mechanical energy into electrical energy for self-powered sensors, wearable electronics, Internet-of-Things devices and distributed energy systems. Although major advances have been made in triboelectric materials, surface engineering and device architectures, the mechanical excitation applied during TENG testing remains an important source of experimental variability. Manual tapping, pressing and sliding can introduce uncontrolled changes in force, displacement, velocity, frequency, contact area and waveform, making comparison between experiments difficult. This review examines cyclical force generation as a controllable subsystem for TENG characterization. Linear actuators, servo systems, electrodynamic shakers, cam-follower and crank-slider mechanisms, electromechanical testing machines and tribometers are compared in terms of force/displacement control, frequency, repeatability, cost and suitability. The review also summarizes the mechanical parameters that should be measured together with electrical output and presents a conceptual closed-loop cyclical force generator (CFG) incorporating an actuator, force sensor, displacement sensor, controller, driver, data-acquisition system and TENG fixture. title: Current-driven Magnetic Skyrmions for Encoding/Storing Information: Manipulation and Dynamics in Nanoscale Structures
abstract: This dissertation investigates the dynamics of current-driven magnetic skyrmions, topological solitons in magnetic materials with broken spatial inversion symmetry, for low-power spintronic applications like racetrack memory and multilevel data storage. Skyrmions’ small size and low driving current requirements make them promising information carriers. The research examines skyrmion motion under driving currents, pinning effects, and thermal fluctuations, using numerical simulations (Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation), analytical studies (Thiele equation), and theoretical modeling to design novel data storage devices. The study analyzes skyrmion motion amidst pinning potentials from material imperfections. Simulations reveal that thermal fluctuations vary with damping: acting as a frictional force at low damping or a driving force aiding depinning at high damping. The Thiele equation quantifies this, though its accuracy wanes at low temperatures with pinning. The skyrmion Hall angle, influenced by current and pinning, provides insights for ambient-condition devices. These findings underpin a proposed multilevel data storage device, where controlled current positions skyrmions at pinning sites for high-density, low-power encoding. The research also explores altermagnetic (ATM) skyrmions, which exhibit d-wave symmetry via exchange-driven spin splitting. title: Study on proppant-fiber cluster structure and settling characteristics for full-domain propped fracturing
journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
abstract: The concept of “full-domain propped fracturing” aims to improve fracture placement morphology by efficient placement in main fractures and hierarchical propping of multi-scale fractures, thereby effectively addressing the limitation of propped fracture volume in unconventional oil and gas reservoirs. Using proppant-fiber clusters instead of pure proppant as the basic transport units in fractures can effectively increase the lateral migration distance and vertical placement height of proppant in main fractures, serving as a key technical approach for achieving efficient fracture placement. This study constructed a physical model of proppant-fiber clusters through microstructural observations, static settling experiments, and dynamic transport experiments, and revealed the settling and placement patterns of cluster units within fractures. The results indicated that proppant-fiber clusters were a composite system jointly composed of a fiber framework that traps proppant particles, a filamentous network of friction reducer polymers, and sheet-like stabilizer structures. Characterization of cluster units and their size distributions revealed that increasing fiber mass fraction and length facilitated the formation of larger cluster units. Specifically, the average proppant placement height increased by 116.6% for a proppant mixture with a fiber mass fraction of 0.5% compared with that of pure proppant.
